text.en: Do you have a pet, or have you wished to? If a bird or an animal could speak to you, who would you pick, and what would you ask? In this story by Hugh Lofting, a doctor learns the language of animals and becomes the most famous doctor in the world for them.

You think about whether you have a pet or a domestic animal and how people spend time with them, and who you would like to speak to if you could talk to an animal or a bird. You also study pictures of animals and birds and work out what their body language tells us about how they feel.
Doctor Dolittle is in his kitchen with the Cat's-food-Man, who came with a stomach-ache. The man suggests that the doctor should give up being a people's doctor and become an animal doctor. He explains that the doctor knows more about animals than the vets do. He cannot read or write himself, but his wife Theodosia, a scholar, read the doctor's book about cats to him, and he felt the doctor knew how cats think. The parrot Polynesia, who has been sitting in the window singing a sailor song, stops and listens. When the man leaves she flies to the table and agrees. She says the doctor should give up the silly people who cannot see he is the best doctor in the world, and look after animals. The doctor says there are plenty of animal doctors. Polynesia says none of them are any good.
Polynesia asks whether he knew that animals can talk. He knew parrots can. She says parrots speak in two languages, people's language and bird language. She says something in bird language, which means Is the porridge hot yet? The doctor is surprised and says she had never spoken that way before. She says it would have been no use because he would not have understood. Excited, he rushes for a book and a pencil to write down the Birds' A.B.C., the language that birds speak. She goes on to teach him body language too. A dog, for example, twitches up one side of his nose to ask a question, which here means Can't you see that it has stopped raining? With the parrot's help the doctor learns the animals' language so well that he can talk to them and understand everything, and he gives up being a people's doctor altogether.
A plough horse is going blind in one eye. The doctor gets a pair of big green spectacles for him, and the horse sees as well as ever. The horse asks for green ones because they will keep the sun out of his eyes while ploughing. The horse adds that anyone thinks he can doctor animals because animals do not complain, but a really good animal doctor needs to be much cleverer than a good people's doctor. Farm animals wearing glasses become a common sight around Puddleby, and a blind horse becomes unknown. Because he can talk to them, animals tell him where it hurts, so it is easy for him to cure them. They tell their friends. Horses, cows, dogs, harvest mice, badgers and bats all come. His garden is crowded, so he has special doors made, with HORSES over the front door, COWS over the side door and SHEEP over the kitchen door. The mice get a tiny tunnel into the cellar. Birds who fly to other countries in winter tell animals abroad about him. He becomes famous among animals all over the world, and he is happy and likes his life very much.
The Cat's-food-Man suggests the change because he believes the doctor knows more about animals than the local vets do. The doctor reacts to Polynesia with excitement and curiosity, and rushes to write down the bird words. In order, the events are: the man visits with a stomach-ache, Polynesia encourages the doctor and reveals animals can talk, she teaches him the languages, he decides to be an animal doctor, the plough horse gets green spectacles, he can diagnose and treat animals well, word spreads, special doors are made, and he gains fame all over the world. The expression Good Gracious shows surprise, and could be replaced by gosh. The doctor feels surprised. Polynesia never used bird language before because he would not have understood. The plough horse's remark shows that people take animals for granted because they cannot complain. The doctor's attitude is respectful and understanding. A challenge of a crowded garden is solved by separate doors.
The writer uses humour, as in animals wearing spectacles and doors marked with animal names. Humour makes the story light and enjoyable. Words in the text include scholar, a learned person; cracker, a thin dry biscuit; countryside, a rural area; and cellar, a room below ground level. (additional, not in the textbook) Direct speech is shown in quotation marks and is changed into reported speech when we tell what someone said, with changes of tense and pronoun, for example Polynesia said that parrots could talk in two languages.

problem.en: Put in order: (a) the doctor learns animal languages; (b) the man with a stomach-ache visits; (c) special doors are built.

text.en: Find the first event.

why.en: The visit with the stomach-ache comes first.

text.en: Then the learning, then the doors.

problem.en: Which word means a learned person?

text.en: Look at the glossary.
Check the story.

why.en: Theodosia, the wife of the Cat's-food-Man, is a scholar.

prompt.en: Tell the story of Doctor Dolittle in your own words and explain how he became famous.

requiredIdeas.en: The Cat's-food-Man and Polynesia suggest he become an animal doctor.
He cures animals, who tell their friends, and special doors are made.
Birds spread his fame around the world.

commonMisconceptions.en: Doctor Dolittle was a vet in a city.
He learned animal language from a book.

points.en: Doctor Dolittle gives up being a people's doctor and becomes an animal doctor.
Polynesia the parrot teaches him that animals can talk.
Spectacles for a plough horse and special doors for animals add humour.
He becomes famous among animals all over the world.
Humour and detail make the fantasy story enjoyable.
